How to read a signal
  1. 📈 TREND BREAKOUT means the price had been climbing and has just pushed to a new high. It happened within the last hour.
  2. Entry is the price when the signal appeared. Price now is where it is right now.
  3. Stop is your exit if it goes wrong. It is a trailing stop: it follows the price up and stays the shown % below the highest price. On Binance, place a Trailing Stop order and enter that % as the trailing delta (Binance allows 0.1% to 20%).
  4. There is no target price. You leave when the trailing stop is hit. In the back-test, trades lasted about 4 days. That is history, not a promise.
  5. Details shows extra numbers (optional). ☆ Follow saves the coin to My Picks.
These signals are not proven to make money. Use small amounts, and judge them by their record in Performance.

glossary.CPI: Consumer Price Index. A measure of how much the prices of everyday goods and services are changing.
glossary.PPI: Producer Price Index. A measure of how much prices are changing for businesses (before they reach shoppers).
glossary.GDP: Gross Domestic Product. The total value of everything a country produces; the main measure of economic growth.
glossary.FOMC: Federal Open Market Committee. The group at the US Federal Reserve that votes on interest rates.
glossary.PMI: Purchasing Managers' Index. A survey of businesses: above 50 means expansion, below 50 means shrinking.
glossary.NFP: Non-Farm Payrolls. The monthly count of new US jobs (the main part of the jobs report).
glossary.PCE: Personal Consumption Expenditures. An inflation measure that the Fed officially targets.
glossary.Jobless Claims: How many people applied for unemployment benefits that week; a quick read on the job market.
glossary.Fed Funds Rate: The main interest rate the US Federal Reserve sets; it influences all other borrowing costs.
glossary.Yield: The return you earn on a bond. When bond prices fall, yields rise (and the reverse).
glossary.Inflation: How fast prices are rising. The Fed aims for about 2% a year.
glossary.Interest Rate: The price of borrowing money. Higher rates make loans and mortgages costlier and usually cool the economy.
glossary.Volatility: How much and how fast a price moves. High volatility means bigger, faster swings.
glossary.Risk assets: Investments that tend to rise when investors feel confident, such as stocks and crypto.
glossary.Consensus: The average forecast of analysts before a data release.
glossary.bp: Basis point. One hundredth of a percentage point (25 bp = 0.25%).

context.author: Crypto Dada (@YTCryptoDada)
context.claim: Higher US yields are read as weak demand for US debt (buyers stepping away from USD assets) rather than economic strength, competition for capital or geopolitics, which are the reasons cited by the Fed side. Raising rates to attract buyers may not work if nobody is buying, and the central bank buying its own bonds is seen as a sign of that weakness.
context.implication: The view expects markets to be held up until the US midterm elections, with an outside shock (for example from Japan's or China's central bank/bond selling) being the main way that changes.
context.how_to_use: Treat as a macro lens for rate-driven events: if yields rise after a hawkish surprise, ask whether it is growth or falling demand for debt. Confirm with data (auction results, yield moves) before acting.

context.author: Crypto Dada (@YTCryptoDada)
context.claim: After an FOMC decision, watch two things: (1) the bond market - if US02Y and US10Y yields fall after the decision, the market tends to react bullishly; (2) the decision versus consensus - a decision that is unexpected (for example a pause when a hike was the consensus) would be a surprise and can move markets sharply. He also flagged upcoming cycle dates and Bank of Japan rate hikes as further catalysts.
context.implication: Rate-path surprises and the yield reaction matter more than the decision itself.
context.how_to_use: After the release, check whether 2Y and 10Y yields rose or fell (Big Coins watchlist) and whether the outcome matched the CME FedWatch probabilities you recorded; a yield drop plus a surprise is the pattern he calls out.

context.author: Crypto Dada (@YTCryptoDada)

context.implication: Big bottoms are expected to follow the start of a cutting cycle, not precede it.
context.how_to_use: A long-horizon lens for cycle context only; it says nothing about the next hours or days.

context.author: Crypto Dada (@YTCryptoDada)
context.claim: His one-word answer to what drives markets is policy: easing or tightening. Monetary policy is the Fed's and fiscal policy is the government's, and more money flowing into an asset (for example legal, easy access to crypto) means more participants and more money.
context.implication: Liquidity direction (easing versus tightening) is the master variable in his framework.
context.how_to_use: Read Fed and inflation events through 'is policy easing or tightening' before reading the chart.

context.author: Crypto Dada (@YTCryptoDada)
context.claim: Article 'Bitcoin cycle: this time is NOT different'. He says he sold over 80% of his spot bags in Aug 2025 near $124k (not the Altcoins, which he says lost most of their value), and had warned of market complacency since Nov 2025. His framework: 'Anticipate, don't chase'. Weekly drops of 35% or more are normal for Bitcoin, and the emotional path after a top is fear, then panic, anger and depression, with capitulation still to come when he wrote it. He suggested only 10-20% invested in the $58-62k zone to control FOMO, no DCA without understanding when and how, no shitcoins in this cycle ('assets the white collars decided to pump' did well), and said you don't need the exact bottom (last cycle he called for buying 20-30% at $16,670). He named quantum computing as a long-term threat to the code.
context.implication: Patience: scale in small near fear zones, wait for capitulation, favour large institution-backed assets over small alts.
context.how_to_use: A cycle lens written in Feb 2026 when BTC was near $60k; BTC has since moved, so treat the price zones as dated and use the framework (small first tranche, wait for capitulation, avoid chasing) rather than the numbers.
